title: Remembering Peter Max
summary: The artist, with his joyful works, created a distinctive visual language.
body_markdown:
[Protect Our Children Ver. II, 2002, by Peter Max](https://www.1stdibs.com/art/prints-works-on-paper/figurative-prints-works-on-paper/peter-max-protect-our-children-ver-ii-peter-max/id-a_13342092/)


Artists who enjoy great commercial success during their lifetimes are often disdained by art world elites. Think of[Andy Warhol](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/andy-warhol/art/) , who was seen by some critics, curators and collectors as too commercial, too ubiquitous and too ambitious to be taken seriously.


[Peter Max in His Studio , 1970, by Michael K. Yamaoka](https://www.1stdibs.com/art/photography/color-photography/michael-k-yamaoka-american-contemporary-photo-michael-yamaoka-peter-max-his-studio/id-a_11443232/)


Much the same was said about the artist[Peter Max](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/peter-max/art/) , who died on September 21 at the age of 88. Although the reach and breadth of his output never quite approached that of Warhol’s, Max, like Warhol, created a distinctive visual language, one that still defines the psychedelic, peace-drugs-love-and-rock-and-roll youth-culture of the 1960s.


[New Moon Detail , 2008, by Peter Max](https://www.1stdibs.com/art/paintings/figurative-paintings/peter-max-new-moon-detail/id-a_14443002/)


Rainbows, stars, flowers and fluffy clouds adorned his images of cosmic runners, lovely ladies in profile and iconic figures (from Bob Dylan to the Statue of Liberty). These appeared on countless dorm-room posters, billboards, album covers, coffee mugs, T-shirts and more, at a time when Pop artists like Warhol and[Roy Lichtenstein](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/roy-lichtenstein/art/) , the subject of a forthcoming blockbuster exhibition at New York’s Whitney Museum, were blurring the line between commercial and fine art.


[On a Distant Planet, 1979, by Peter Max](https://www.1stdibs.com/art/prints-works-on-paper/figurative-prints-works-on-paper/peter-max-on-distant-planet-peter-max/id-a_12181472/)


Brightly colored and inherently happy, the works today feel nostalgic — harking back to the ’60s, of course, and even earlier, to the Art Nouveau period at the start of the 20th century. But they also feel timely and inspiriting: a dose of zippy, trippy joy for any dark or daunting day.
